Stardew Valley is one of those games that I will always come back to, no matter how much time has passed. I have over 200 hours on PC alone, and I couldn't even begin to guess how many more I've spent playing on Switch! No matter how many times I start a new farm, there is always something new to discover, another goal to work toward, or another reason to fall in love with the game all over again.

The amount of content is genuinely incredible. Between the overarching story, the countless quests, the secrets to uncover, and the individual stories and relationships of each NPC, there is always something to do. Every character feels unique, with their own personality, struggles, interests, and growth. Getting to know the villagers and seeing their stories unfold makes Pelican Town feel like a real community rather than just a setting for a farming game.

And the farming itself? There is genuinely something for every type of player! Whether you love growing crops, fishing, mining, raising animals, ranching, crafting artisan goods, decorating, or focusing on relationships and exploration, the game gives you so much freedom to play however you want. You can spend an entire day optimizing your farm, disappear into the mines for hours, or simply wander around town talking to everyone. There's no single right way to play, and I love that.

What makes Stardew Valley especially special to me is how comforting it is. It's the kind of game you can pick up when you need something familiar and relaxing, lose yourself in for hours, and return to months or even years later without losing that feeling of coming home. There's always another season to experience, another project to finish, or another little detail to appreciate.

And I genuinely cannot praise ConcernedApe enough for what he has created. It's amazing to see a game made with so much heart continue to grow and bring joy to so many people.

This game has a lot of content and it took me a long time to beat.  When I say "beat," I mean "perfect."  Because the only way to really beat the game is to 100% it, which is very time-consuming.

There's not really much of a story except for at the beginning.  Otherwise, you basically just build up your life, family, friends and town.  There are really only two mutually exclusive choices to make, but they mostly lead to similar outcomes, and the rewards are different.

When starting the game, you can choose what kind of farm you want between a regular farm, beach farm, a forage farm, a farm with monsters, etc.  The goal is still the same; sow, harvest, get paid.

I lost track of how many quests there were, mostly because a lot of them repeat.  If I were to summarize it into different parts, I'd limit it to the following:  Farming, mining, relationships and community.

Farming is what you would think; grow crops, build coops and stables, care for animals, produce artisan goods, craft stuff, cook dishes, etc.

Mining is more of the adventurous and combative part of the game where you explore the floors of mines, fight enemies, find rare resources and artifacts, forge, find and upgrade weapons, etc.

Relationships involve the local and non-local citizens.  Talking to them, gifting them things they like or completing quests for them increase your relationship.  In contrast, saying mean things, hitting trashcans in front of them, or gifting them things they don't like will decrease your relationship.  There are events that happen at various times and places once you've reached a certain relationship threshold with a particular person and it reveals a little more depth to their lives and develops their character further.  There are bachelors and bachelorettes that can be romanced and eventually married, after which they move in with you, enabling you to have/adopt up to 2 children.  Some of this cannot be done until you've upgraded your house sufficiently.  There are a number of characters that are either already married or cannot otherwise be romanced.  There are mods that can change this, FYI.  I didn't use any of them, for the record.

The community-related part of the game involves developments that improve things around town, like fixing buses, boats or bridges that lead to new places, fixing the greenhouse on your property for indoor farming, removing rocks so that ore and minerals flow through the town's water, etc.  This is the part where there are two mutually exclusive ways to go about it.  The developer has made it very apparent that one of these ways is their preferred way, and is a lot more in-depth and time-consuming in nature.  The other way is more efficient, but is made to feel more empty in the end.  Some of the new places revealed by these developments are beyond the local town, and there are different caves, mines, farms, people and quests to work with.  Like I said, this game has a lot of content.

I can see why so many people like this game.  I'd say the unfortunate part for me was that I got overwhelmed at one point and had to put it down.  I came back a few years later to complete it.  It's difficult to do this, however, because I had to remember how everything worked and how I left things originally. 

Anyway, I think most adventure gamers, or people who like games such as Terraria or Minecraft would enjoy this game a lot.

Act 1: Absolutely amazing. The absolute peak of RPG gaming.

Act 2: Still good, but the cracks are starting to show.

Act 3: An incomprehensible clusterfuck where everything pretends to matter, but somehow nothing feels particularly impactful anymore.

Baldur's Gate 3 starts off as one of the most incredible RPG experiences I've ever had. Act 1 is genuinely fantastic. The exploration, the companions, the choices, the feeling that you're just a bunch of adventurers trying to make sense of the world around you. It's everything I want from an RPG.

Act 2 is still good, but things start feeling increasingly railroaded. Misinterpret one little thing, make a decision without fully understanding its consequences, and suddenly something massive happens that can sour the rest of your campaign. Player agency starts feeling less like freedom and more like trying to guess what the writers intended you to do.

And then comes Act 3.

Good lord, what happened here?

Suddenly you're drowning in supposedly world-shattering revelations, grand conspiracies, and characters with increasingly ridiculous ambitions. Everything is presented as the most important thing imaginable, yet very little of it actually feels meaningful.

It's like starting out reading The Fellowship of the Ring, embarking on this wonderful, grounded adventure with a group of companions, only for the story to slowly transform into some American Gods-style drama where the biggest, strongest, most important beings in existence all have the biggest, meanest plans.

And of course, you and your merry band of increasingly overpowered superheroes are the only ones who can stop them.

Somewhere along the way, the grounded RPG adventure turns into a comical superhero flick.

And perhaps the funniest part is that, in doing so, Baldur's Gate 3 stays remarkably faithful to D&D 5e.

Because it suffers from exactly the same progression problem: you start out as a bunch of nobodies worrying about goblins stealing someone's chickens, and before you know it, you're fighting gods, dragons, and the equivalent of World War III because apparently every adventure needs to escalate into a cosmic catastrophe.

Bigger stakes, bigger villains, bigger explosions. But not necessarily a better story.

I wish Baldur's Gate 3 had remained the adventure it was in Act 1. A wonderful, personal journey where your companions, discoveries, and smaller decisions felt like they mattered.

Instead, it trades that magic for an increasingly bloated spectacle that seems convinced the fate of the entire universe is inherently more interesting than the fate of a handful of adventurers.

An absolutely phenomenal beginning, a decent middle, and a final act that completely lost me.

Sometimes saving a village from goblins is a far better adventure than saving the entire world from gods.

Let's get one thing out of the way before I say anything: I adore this game. I adore the combat, the story, all the characters, and that I'm still finding new things in every playthrough. I'm on my 8th playthrough right now. You can see how many hours I have in this game. At the time of writing this review I have three more playthroughs planned not including the one I'm currently on. None have been boring and every single one has been different. I've played this game every three months since its release.

Now, would I recommend this game to other players? It depends.

Do you enjoy an intricate story with lots of character customization and role playing possibilities but don't care for intricate combat? Play this game and play it on the easiest difficulty. Look up builds so you know which abilities to pick and what gear to buy. Get mods to make your player character look even wackier or make them nigh invincible so the combat is peanuts. Romance your favorite companion and then make a new character and romance them again. Explore what happens when you fail a roll. Save scum if you don't like the outcome. Play your favorite character's origin and make them smooch another origin character, or your guardian. Make their guardian look like your player character. Take screenshots. Frame your favorites. Go wild. 

Do you enjoy strategy turn based combat that has a variety of ways to solve fights, challenging bosses and hours of enormous battles with 20+ participants, but don't care for elaborate party management, pesky approval ratings and their consequences, and don't care for role playing in general? Play this game on Tactician and only use hirelings, don't recruit any companions. Try honor mode and enjoy the adrenaline rush. Min-max your heart out. Do a challenge run. (Also definitely try the previous game from Larian; Divinity Original Sin 2 if you enjoy this type of combat.)

However. Do you not care for elaborate roleplay worth hundreds of hours over multiple playthroughs, long cutscenes and romance mechanics, or any form of turn-based strategy games? Then there's thousands of other games for you out there. But probably not this one.

Or, you know, get it on sale some time and give it a go anyway. Broaden your horizons.

10/10 - A must play for all gamers

GAMEPLAY
--------------

As close to perfect RPG gameplay as we have ever seen. Every single situation can be resolved in what feels like thousands of ways. Whether it's ridiculous cheese or clever party tactics. The roleplay potential is incredible, with every race, class, and then subclass having unique dialogue/in-dialogue action options in many conversations. The build variety is amazing, especially with multi-classing. You can go the traditional Warlock/Wizard caster or Barbarian Bruiser route; or whip out the excel sheet and create a multi-class demon that excels at your ultra-specific playstyle. Considering you can have 3 other party members, this adds so much gameplay/combat potential that it'll make your head spin if you try to consider all the possibilities. You can approach encounters in pretty much anyway you want; whether that's teleporting targets in-between your damage dealers, going invis for stealth, shapeshifting, sending someone to talk to the target while you attack their allies, dropping 50 fire barrels from your inventory on their head, spamming arrows from the high ground, cheesing them with CC, the list goes on forever. There is definitely a learning curve if you have never played D&D or the like, but starting the game on "Easy" and watching a YT video is really all you need. I recommend playing a little first, then watching a video, as the terms and info dump are hard to contextualize without exp in-game.

STORY
--------------

But a massive RPG is dependent on it's story and companions. BG3 has excellent female companions, with Lae'zel and Shadowheart being the most interesting and with the best questlines. The other recruitable female companions are good too, with interesting backstories and dialogue options. And this is all without their romance questlines, which are all quite well-done. But the male companions are where the game kind of suffers. Gale, Astarion, and Wyll especially, are just kind of annoying. Their questlines are all pretty interesting so it is worth completing them, but I found myself leaving them in camp in further runs. They come on to you pretty quickly as well, even if you are already progressing another party members romance. These companions never really hinder the game, but I definitely would have preferred a few more stoic, less quippy type male characters. There is a companion you can recruit who is a bit more serious, but that is late into the game. Regardless, completing your parties questlines and hearing their interactions with you and others were some of my favorite moments in the narrative. There is a very immersive element to hearing your party members talk to each other and mention their surroundings or past events without your input. 

The main story is great, with the voice acting and character models being stellar. I would have preferred a slower or more grounded start to the game and overall story, but that is just personal preference and others might enjoy a more epic fantasy tale which the game has. The ending cutscenes feel a little rushed and it would have been great to have more options when it comes to who you have to fight, but these are pretty excusable considering the rest of the games story. 


OVERALL
------------

As a longtime Gears fan who has played every game multiple times since 2012, I absolutely love this game.

This game has it all. The movement is incredibly smooth and honestly rivals games like TLOU2, the weapons feel great, and the story is fantastic. Seeing Marcus and Dom back together again is great, and I really like the new characters too. They might not be as iconic as Baird, Cole, and Anya, but they're still great additions to the series.

I also really like how they've experimented with a more open approach in certain sections. Being able to revisit previous areas and see how much more destroyed they become as the story progresses is such a cool detail. The boss fights have been really fun, and getting to experience the origins of the Locust War has been a highlight.

Now, I think it's only fair to address some of the complaints I've seen about this game.

First off, this game is not "woke." The game includes optional banners and flags that you can equip if you want to. That's it. If something as simple as optional cosmetics is enough to make you not recommend or not want to play a game, then honestly, you shouldn't be playing games.

I've also seen a lot of people complaining that The Coalition gives Lucas and Mags too much focus, which is just straight-up not true. Mags gets maybe five minutes of focus in a campaign that's over 12 hours long. The additional character details also make sense when you consider that the campaign now supports four-player co-op instead of the two-player co-op of the older games. Giving the new characters actual personalities and backstories makes it easier for players to care about whoever they're playing as. I really don't see the problem here.

As for the multiplayer, Versus is solid. Nothing particularly groundbreaking, but it's good. Horde is fun too, although I personally prefer how it was handled in the older games.

Now, for my dislikes, which honestly aren't many. I do think it was a mistake to remove some of the features that made the older games so unique. Meatshields, unique weapon executions, Lancer battles, and grenade tagging are all awesome mechanics that I wish had returned. These features added a lot of personality to the combat, and I would've loved to see them make a comeback.

That said, none of these complaints come close to ruining the experience for me.

I'd give this game a 9.5/10. The story is great, the characters are great, the movement feels fantastic, the weapons are satisfying, and the gameplay is just incredibly fun. It manages to feel like Gears of War while still trying new things, and I think The Coalition has done a fantastic job with it.

I'm extremely happy with what they've delivered. I really don't have any major complaints, and I can't wait to see where the series goes from here.

[h1] When everything works, the game is great. Unfortunately, nothing ever really fully works. [/h1]

I'll add some context here: this is the first FIFA/FC I've played in around 4–5 years, so coming back to the series has genuinely been fun. However, the sheer amount of technical issues is, quite honestly, embarrassing.

You'd think that after making essentially the same game every year for well over 20 years, something as simple as the menus actually working would be a fair expectation, but apparently not.

Other issues include the game randomly deciding, after starting a match, that you're now playing with MnK instead of your controller. The best part? The controller will still work perfectly fine in the menus, just not in the actual match. The amount of times the only solution to something in this game is to simply turn it off and back on again is astounding.

Then there's the servers. Every 4–5 games, they'll seemingly just collapse, and you'll be handed a loss regardless of whether you were winning or not. I've even had a game where I was 3–0 up, my opponent left, and somehow [b] I was handed the loss?[/b] Where is the logic in that?

The new co-op mode, "The Grounds", is actually a lot of fun, but again, it comes with the usual preface of [i]"when it works"[/i], which seems to be a 50/50 coin flip every time you launch it. The stability in The Grounds is shocking as well. Random frame drops down to 20–30 FPS before shooting straight back up to 100+, regardless of how high or low your graphics settings are. There is seemingly no rhyme or reason to it.

I write all of this knowing full well that I'll continue playing because, underneath all the issues, I am genuinely having fun with the game. When everything is working as intended, it's a fun game.

But in terms of recommending that someone else spends their money on it? [u]Absolutely not.[/u]

I can't buy the whole [i]"Oh well, it's an EA game, what do you expect?"[/i] excuse either. At the end of the day I have paid for a game that can barely manage to function consistently, despite being an annual release from one of the biggest publishers in the industry.

It's a shambles the majority of the time, the fact that there's a genuinely enjoyable game buried underneath all of it just makes it that much more frustrating.
